title: Understand space groups, double groups and magnetic groups through typical materials

sources.title: AFLOW：Rock Salt/Halite (NaCl, B1) Structure
sources.note: Official prototype library: verify Fm-3m, fcc translations, and two site sets differing by (1/2,1/2,1/2). The model places Na at the origin; a  origin choice  exchanging chemical motifs does not change the  space group  type.

sources.title: AFLOW：Diamond (A4) Structure
sources.note: Official prototype library checking the diamond structure, Si isotypes and No.227. This page uses origin choice 2; the lesson shifts the origin to a Si atom and uses the common basis 0 and (1/4,1/4,1/4).

sources.title: AFLOW：Zincblende (B3) Structure
sources.note: Official prototype library, verifying No.216 and tetrahedral coordination of two atom types. The GaAs model selects Ga at 4a and As at 4c.

sources.title: AFLOW：Body-Centered Cubic (A2, bcc) Structure
sources.note: Official prototype library: verify bcc nuclear positions and No.229; this teaching model specifies the  ferromagnetic  direction separately.

sources.title: AFLOW：Rutile (TiO2, C4) Structure
sources.note: Official rutile prototype, checking the 2a/4f fractional coordinates of No.136; used for the chemical structure type of MnF2.

sources.title: Stout & Reed (1954)：The Crystal Structure of MnF2, FeF2, CoF2, NiF2 and ZnF2
sources.note: Original X-ray structural study: MnF2 is rutile at 25°C with a=4.8734 Å, c=3.3099 Å, u=0.310(3). The lesson uses rounded c/a=0.68 and u=0.310, not a low-temperature refinement.

sources.title: Yamani, Tun & Ryan (2010)：Neutron scattering study of the classical antiferromagnet MnF2
sources.note: Original neutron-scattering teaching experiment supporting antiparallel c-axis moments on the two rutile Mn sublattices. Ligand moments and finite-temperature fluctuations neglected here are not claimed to be strict experimental zeros.

sources.title: Roth (1958)：Magnetic Structures of MnO, FeO, CoO, and NiO
sources.note: Original neutron-diffraction study supporting antiferromagnetically stacked (111) ferromagnetic planes and in-plane moments in NiO.

sources.title: Pomjakushin (2024)：On the magnetic and crystal structures of NiO and MnO
sources.note: Original diffraction study discussing low-temperature lattice distortion and discrimination of magnetic-structure models. An ideal cubic parent phase or a few operations cannot replace experimental magnetic-group refinement.

sources.title: Weber et al. (2024)：Surface Magnetization in Antiferromagnets: Classification, Example Materials, and Relation to Magnetoelectric Responses
sources.note: The NiO case uses (111) layers and in-plane [11-2] moments, selecting one ideal magnetic domain for the lesson.

sources.title: Elcoro et al. (2017)：Double crystallographic groups and their representations on the Bilbao Crystallographic Server
sources.note: Primary methods paper on double groups, SU(2) lifts, and double-valued representations; the spinor derivations below are original teaching examples.

materials.name: Sodium chloride: first identify the chemical motif
materials.phase: Ideal ambient-pressure rock-salt structure; nonmagnetic nuclear-position model

spaceGroup.setting: Cubic F conventional cell; Na at (0,0,0), Cl at (1/2,1/2,1/2)

materials.summary: Different chemical species on the same geometric lattice cannot be exchanged arbitrarily. Use rocksalt to compare face-centering translations with pseudosymmetries exchanging Na and Cl.
materials.physics: space group  preserves the entire species-labeled periodic structure; geometric overlap is only necessary.
limitations: The lattice constant is normalized to 1; temperature, strain and ionic displacements are not fitted.
Zero moments mean this nuclear-structure model has no magnetic order; they do not model instantaneous spin fluctuations.

sections.title: Two fcc sublattices within one  conventional cell
paragraphs: Na occupies the four face-centered lattice points; Cl uses the same coordinates shifted by (1/2,1/2,1/2) and wrapped into the cell. The conventional cell therefore contains 4 Na and 4 Cl.
The face-centering translation (0,1/2,1/2) maps Na to Na and Cl to Cl. Although (1/2,1/2,1/2) preserves the geometric point set, it exchanges elements and is not a NaCl translation symmetry.

sections.title: From demonstration to  space group
paragraphs: A 90° rotation about z and inversion at the origin both preserve the two chemical species. Combining them with face-centering translations explains the geometric information in Fm-3m.
Only a few representative operations are shown. Open the workbench for complete operations and representations in the standard BC setting; the demonstration sample count is not the group order.

model.convention: cell is the matrix A whose columns are Cartesian basis vectors. Fractional coordinates are column vectors, r=A·f. Lengths are normalized by the parent conventional-cell parameter a and have no Å unit. moment is a normalized time-odd axial vector in Cartesian coordinates, not a measured moment in μB. The operations are teaching samples, not a complete space-group list.

operations.label: Identity E
operations.explanation: Leave all atoms in place as the reference for matching positions and chemical species; no rotation or translation is applied.

operations.label: Rotate 90° about z
operations.explanation: Rotate the entire structure by 90° about z. Na still maps to Na and Cl to Cl, demonstrating the fourfold symmetry of the cubic structure.

operations.label: Inversion through the origin
operations.explanation: Replace each fractional coordinate f by −f, allowing integer cell translations. Each chemical sublattice is preserved.

operations.label: Face-centering translation (0,1/2,1/2)
operations.explanation: Translate the whole structure by (0,1/2,1/2). The Na and Cl fcc sublattices each map to themselves, so this is a valid face-centering translation.

operations.label: Counterexample: translation (1/2,1/2,1/2)
operations.explanation: After translation by (1/2,1/2,1/2), the geometric point set overlaps, but Na and Cl are interchanged. The chemical structure is not preserved.

materials.name: Silicon: compensating translation and  double-valued representation
materials.phase: Ideal ambient-pressure diamond structure; no magnetic order

spaceGroup.setting: Cubic F conventional cell, origin choice 1 (on Si); basis 0 and (1/4,1/4,1/4)

materials.summary: Whether rotated atoms coincide depends on the translation part; electron spinors must also retain the minus sign left by a 360° turn.
materials.physics: Nuclear-position spatial symmetry and electronic-spin SU(2) representations describe different freedoms and require separate verification.
limitations: The model places the origin on an atom; do not mix these coordinates directly with origin choice 2 in standard tables.
The double-group derivation illustrates spin-1/2 kinematics only, not actual Si bands or spin–orbit splittings.

sections.title: A translated fourfold operation
paragraphs: With a Si atom at the origin, pure C4z maps (1/4,1/4,1/4) to an empty position. Adding t=(1/4,1/4,1/4) restores a one-to-one mapping of all Si atoms.

The rotation axis of this {C4z|t} is offset from the origin. After four applications its rotation is identity and total translation is (0,0,1). Identical wrapped cell pictures do not make the infinite-crystal operation identity.

sections.title: An inversion center need not be at the origin
paragraphs: {−I|(1/4,1/4,1/4)} has center (1/8,1/8,1/8) and exchanges the two equivalent Si sublattices.
For spin 1/2, a 360° spatial rotation lifts to −I and 720° returns to +I. A 3D atomic animation cannot reveal this overall spinor sign; use the derivation or spinor experiment alongside it.

model.convention: cell is the matrix A whose columns are Cartesian basis vectors. Fractional coordinates are column vectors, r=A·f. Lengths are normalized by the parent conventional-cell parameter a and have no Å unit. moment is a normalized time-odd axial vector in Cartesian coordinates, not a measured moment in μB. The operations are teaching samples, not a complete space-group list.

operations.label: Identity E
operations.explanation: Leave all Si positions unchanged as the reference for other operations. Only nuclear positions are tested here, not spinor phases.

operations.label: Rotate 180° about z
operations.explanation: After a 180° rotation about z, every Si atom has a periodically equivalent Si partner. The corresponding half-turn of an electron spin carries an additional SU(2) factor, which must be calculated in the double-group derivation.

operations.label: Rotate 120° about [111]
operations.explanation: Cyclically permute x, y, and z, equivalent to a 120° rotation about [111]. Both Si sublattices are individually preserved.

operations.label: Inversion center (1/8,1/8,1/8)
operations.explanation: Negate f, then add (1/4,1/4,1/4). This is inversion through (1/8,1/8,1/8). The two sublattices are exchanged, but both contain Si, so the operation passes.

operations.label: {C4z | 1/4,1/4,1/4}
operations.explanation: First rotate 90° about z, then translate by (1/4,1/4,1/4) to compensate the basis-position difference. Four repetitions leave a translation (0,0,1). Folding back into the cell does not make the full operation the identity.

operations.label: Counterexample: C4z alone
operations.explanation: A 90° rotation about the z axis through the current origin sends some Si atoms to empty sites. Without the compensating translation, the structure cannot be matched completely.

materials.name: Gallium arsenide: similar geometry, different symmetry
materials.phase: Ideal ambient-pressure zinc-blende structure; no magnetic order

spaceGroup.setting: Cubic F conventional cell; Ga at 4a, As at 4c

materials.summary: Replace silicon’s two identical-element sublattices with Ga and As: inversion, which exchanged the two sets of basis atoms, no longer survives.
materials.physics: Species occupations reduce spatial symmetry; electronic spin requires the  double group  of the surviving symmetry.
limitations: Only the cubic zinc-blende phase is considered, not the wurtzite phase that may occur in nanowires.
Absence of inversion does not require splitting at every k; time reversal, little groups, and the specific Hamiltonian also matter.

sections.title: Comparing Si and GaAs
paragraphs: Ga and As use the same two geometric coordinate sets as silicon. The bond-center inversion of Si would send Ga to As, so it is absent from this chemical structure’s space group.
A threefold rotation about [111] preserves each element; the z-axis rotoinversion S4z=−C4z also preserves both sublattices. Do not confuse −4 with pure 4.

sections.title: time reversal  and spin degeneracy
paragraphs: Ideal nonmagnetic GaAs with spin–orbit coupling can still have Θ symmetry. For spin 1/2, Θ²=−I directly gives Kramers pairing only when Θ returns k to the same momentum subspace.
The 3D model checks atomic positions. Double-valued representations are checked in the workbench or spinor experiment; coordinates do not contain complete electronic-wavefunction information.

model.convention: cell is the matrix A whose columns are Cartesian basis vectors. Fractional coordinates are column vectors, r=A·f. Lengths are normalized by the parent conventional-cell parameter a and have no Å unit. moment is a normalized time-odd axial vector in Cartesian coordinates, not a measured moment in μB. The operations are teaching samples, not a complete space-group list.

operations.label: Identity E
operations.explanation: Leave Ga and As in place as the reference for matching positions with chemical labels.

operations.label: Rotate 180° about z
operations.explanation: After a 180° rotation about z, Ga maps to Ga and As to As. Each chemical species is preserved, not merely the unlabeled point set.

operations.label: Rotate 120° about [111]
operations.explanation: Cyclically permute x, y, and z, corresponding to a 120° rotation about [111]. The Ga and As sublattices are individually preserved.

operations.label: Fourfold rotoinversion S4z
operations.explanation: Rotate 90° about z, then invert through the origin: S4z=−C4z. This combination preserves the Ga and As sublattices individually; it must be distinguished from a pure fourfold rotation.

operations.label: Face-centering translation
operations.explanation: Translation by (0,1/2,1/2) maps each fcc sublattice to itself and therefore preserves the chemical structure of GaAs.

operations.label: Counterexample: use the Si inversion
operations.explanation: The bond-centered inversion used for Si interchanges Ga and As. The position set overlaps, but the chemical labels are not preserved, so this is not a chemical symmetry of GaAs.

materials.name: Iron: magnetization direction selects symmetry
materials.phase: Ideal ferromagnetic single-domain bcc α-Fe; fixed M∥[001]

spaceGroup.setting: Listed: the bcc chemical parent; cubic I  conventional cell

materials.summary: For the same bcc nuclear structure, fixing magnetization retains only unitary or antiunitary combinations that preserve the moments.
materials.physics: A magnetic moment is a time-odd axial vector, transforming as m′=s det(Q)Qm; inversion leaves it unchanged, while time reversal reverses it.
limitations: Choose an ideal single domain below the ferromagnetic transition with M∥[001]. With SOC, spatial operations also act on moment directions.
Arbitrary  independent spin rotation  are not used as compensation; magnetic-anisotropy energy and temperature dependence are not calculated.
All Fe moments have magnitude 1; Im-3m labels the chemical parent phase and is not claimed to be the magnetic space group of this domain.

sections.title: Nuclear positions may pass while moments fail
paragraphs: The bcc  conventional cell  contains Fe(0,0,0), Fe(1/2,1/2,1/2), both magnetized +z. C2x preserves nuclei but turns moments to −z, breaking the selected domain.

Combining with time reversal Θ reverses the moment a second time, so ΘC2x preserves this ideal magnetic order. The counterexample and valid operation have identical atomic-position animations; their difference lies in the moments.

sections.title: Why inversion preserves magnetization
paragraphs: Inversion has Q=−I, detQ=−1, so axial vectors transform by det(Q)Q=I. Polar-vector positions reverse but moments remain unchanged.

Θ alone preserves every nuclear position but reverses the entire ferromagnetic domain into another domain. “Two domains have equal energy” and “the current domain is preserved” are distinct statements.

model.convention: cell is the matrix A whose columns are Cartesian basis vectors. Fractional coordinates are column vectors, r=A·f. Lengths are normalized by the parent conventional-cell parameter a and have no Å unit. moment is a normalized time-odd axial vector in Cartesian coordinates, not a measured moment in μB. The operations are teaching samples, not a complete space-group list.

operations.label: Identity E
operations.explanation: Leave both Fe positions and their +z moments unchanged as the reference for the selected ferromagnetic domain.

operations.label: Body-centering translation
operations.explanation: Translation by (1/2,1/2,1/2) exchanges the two Fe atoms. Their moments are parallel, so both chemical positions and magnetic order are preserved.

operations.label: Inversion: moments do not reverse
operations.explanation: Inversion negates positions, but a magnetic moment is an axial vector and det(Q)Q=I. The +z moments do not reverse; both positional and magnetic matching pass.

operations.label: Rotate 90° about the magnetization axis
operations.explanation: A 90° rotation about the chosen magnetization axis z preserves the bcc nuclear positions and the +z moments. Its validity depends on the fixed magnetic-domain direction.

operations.label: Counterexample: C2x reverses the moments
operations.explanation: A 180° rotation about x preserves the bcc atomic positions but sends +z moments to −z, breaking the selected ferromagnetic domain.

operations.label: ΘC2x: two sign reversals
operations.explanation: C2x first sends the moments to −z; time reversal reverses them again to +z. Spatial positions and magnetic moments both match.

operations.label: Counterexample: time reversal Θ alone
operations.explanation: Time reversal leaves the nuclei in place but sends all +z moments to −z. It maps the selected domain to the opposite magnetic domain rather than preserving its magnetic order.

materials.name: Nickel oxide: antitranslation and the magnetic cell
materials.phase: An AF-II layered  antiferromagnetic  single domain on ideal rocksalt (AF-II denotes order, not a type-II gray group)

spaceGroup.setting: Chemical parent-phase label; the demonstration uses a nonorthogonal magnetic primitive cell of volume a³/2

materials.summary: Adjacent  ferromagnetic  planes along [111] alternate their moments. A chemical translation may break magnetic order, while  time reversal  combined with that translation restores it.
materials.physics: The magnetic translation lattice can be a subgroup of the chemical translation lattice. Do not mix their reciprocal-space coordinates.
limitations: Choose single-Q domain Q=(1/2,1/2,1/2) in parent cubic  conventional cell   reciprocal lattice  basis units, with normalized m∥[11-2]. Induced oxygen moments are neglected.
Actual low-temperature NiO has a small lattice distortion; this example freezes the ideal cubic parent structure and cannot replace measured structural refinement or a unique MSG assignment.
Moment directions are SOC-locked; independent spin rotations cannot compensate spatial operations.

sections.title: From fcc chemical  primitive cell  to magnetic  primitive cell
paragraphs: Let a1=(0,1/2,1/2), a2=(1/2,0,1/2), a3=(1/2,1/2,0), in units of the cubic parent lattice constant a. Choose b1=a1−a2, b2=a2−a3, b3=a1+a2.

The Ni moment at chemical translation n1a1+n2a2+n3a3 has sign (−1)^(n1+n2+n3). All three b translations preserve the sign, so the magnetic primitive cell accommodates two opposite Ni moments and two O atoms.

sections.title: Why ΘTτ can hold
paragraphs: τ=a1 has coordinates (1/2,0,1/2) in the new magnetic cell. Tτ exchanges the two Ni sublattices without actively reversing moments, so it is not a symmetry of the magnetic order; ΘTτ also reverses moments, restoring a one-to-one match.

In this model inversion preserves each magnetic sublattice's sign, but Θ alone fails to preserve the domain. The 3D plot uses a nonorthogonal cell to show actual geometry; fractional coordinates must not be treated directly as Cartesian arrows.

model.convention: cell is the matrix A whose columns are Cartesian basis vectors. Fractional coordinates are column vectors, r=A·f. Lengths are normalized by the parent conventional-cell parameter a and have no Å unit. moment is a normalized time-odd axial vector in Cartesian coordinates, not a measured moment in μB. The operations are teaching samples, not a complete space-group list. The three columns of this A are b1,b2,b3; fractional τ=(1/2,0,1/2) corresponds to Cartesian a1=(0,1/2,1/2).

operations.label: Identity E
operations.explanation: Leave all atoms and moments in the nonorthogonal magnetic primitive cell unchanged as the reference for the chosen AF-II domain.

operations.label: Inversion through the origin
operations.explanation: After inversion through the origin, atoms still match periodically with the same species. Axial-vector moments do not reverse under inversion, so this ideal magnetic order is preserved.

operations.label: Counterexample: chemical translation τ alone
operations.explanation: Translation by magnetic-cell fractional coordinates τ=(1/2,0,1/2) matches every chemical position, but exchanges the two Ni magnetic sublattices without reversing their moments. Magnetic order is not preserved.

operations.label: Antitranslation ΘTτ
operations.explanation: The same translation exchanges the oppositely aligned Ni sublattices; time reversal then reverses their moments and restores the complete match. This antitranslation is preserved by the magnetic order.

operations.label: Counterexample: Θ alone
operations.explanation: Time reversal alone preserves nuclear positions but reverses the moment on every Ni. A zero net moment does not imply that Θ preserves the selected antiferromagnetic domain.

materials.name: Manganese difluoride: ligands determine  antiferromagnetic  symmetry
materials.phase: Ambient-pressure rutile-type collinear antiferromagnetic single domain; Mn moments along ±c

spaceGroup.setting: Tetragonal P chemical conventional cell; Mn at 2a, F at 4f

materials.summary: Looking only at two Mn atoms incorrectly suggests a half-translation symmetry. Including F ligands requires a combined rotation and translation to preserve the complete chemical structure.
materials.physics: Magnetic symmetry requires position and moment matching for every species; the complete magnetic group cannot be guessed from magnetic atoms alone.
limitations: The model fixes u=0.310 and c/a=0.68, rounded for teaching from the ambient-pressure structure rather than low-temperature refined values.
Specify an ideal zero-field ±c single domain below the antiferromagnetic transition, retaining SOC constraints on direction and neglecting induced ligand moments and small distortions.
No.136 is the chemical-parent  space group ; the few listed operations are not a complete magnetic-group classification.

sections.title: All six atoms must be checked
paragraphs: Mn sites are (0,0,0) and (1/2,1/2,1/2), with +z and −z moments. Four F sites are (u,u,0), (−u,−u,0), (1/2−u,1/2+u,1/2), (1/2+u,1/2−u,1/2).
Pure (1/2,1/2,1/2) translation exchanges Mn but fails to map all F to F, so it is not chemical symmetry. Adding Θ cannot repair ligand positions.

sections.title: Rotation, translation and time reversal each play a distinct role
paragraphs: g={C4z|(1/2,1/2,1/2)} exchanges both Mn atoms and correctly maps all four F atoms. But C4z does not reverse z moments, so g breaks the selected antiferromagnetic order.
Θg first rearranges atoms spatially, then reverses moments, matching both. This explains errors caused by drawing Mn without F.

model.convention: cell is the matrix A whose columns are Cartesian basis vectors. Fractional coordinates are column vectors, r=A·f. Lengths are normalized by the parent conventional-cell parameter a and have no Å unit. moment is a normalized time-odd axial vector in Cartesian coordinates, not a measured moment in μB. The operations are teaching samples, not a complete space-group list.

operations.label: Identity E
operations.explanation: Leave both Mn atoms, all four F atoms, and the chosen ±c moments unchanged as the reference for the complete six-atom model.

operations.label: Inversion through the origin
operations.explanation: Inversion through the origin correctly permutes F and preserves the periodic Mn positions. Magnetic moments are axial vectors and do not reverse under inversion, so the magnetic order is preserved.

operations.label: Rotate 180° about c
operations.explanation: A 180° rotation about c exchanges F sites in pairs and preserves the Mn sites and z-directed moments. Both chemical and magnetic matching pass.

operations.label: Counterexample: {C4z|1/2,1/2,1/2}
operations.explanation: Rotate 90° about c, then add (1/2,1/2,1/2). All Mn and F positions are preserved, but the two exchanged Mn moments have not reversed. Only chemical matching passes.

operations.label: Θ{C4z|1/2,1/2,1/2}
operations.explanation: Rotation and translation first correctly permute Mn and F. Time reversal then reverses the Mn moments to match those on the target sublattice.

operations.label: Counterexample: pure half translation
operations.explanation: A pure half translation exchanges the two Mn atoms but cannot match all four F ligands. Considering only magnetic atoms would misidentify this operation.

operations.label: Counterexample: Θ plus pure half translation
operations.explanation: Adding Θ to the pure half translation reverses the Mn moments, but Θ does not move nuclei and cannot repair the mismatched F-ligand positions.
